name: Emeka Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What's your factory line?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Emeka, 58, and I lead the corrugated-board laminator line that bonds paper layers for shipping cartons. I have a two-year technical diploma in production machinery and sixteen years on this line. I can tune heat and glue across a wide board and teach the crew to spot bubbles before a pallet is spoiled.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are pay, family and your use of AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Marek works at a post-office counter, and our grown children have moved out. My lead wage is typical for this kind of factory job, we have about three months of expenses saved, and a few other packaging plants are reachable. I use AI every day to search manuals and organise fault logs, then check a bonded board against the approved specification. I like trying a new control early on a guarded test run. I support union bargaining so a course is paid for every shift, not only day managers. Retirement sounds possible one day, but we have not costed written income against our household needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the laminator crew that quicker order paperwork could keep the right paper rolls arriving. The bonded board still has to pass a peel test before I release a pallet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wages and three months saved cover normal bills. Office AI does not alter the heat, glue or physical roll handling, so I do not expect this change to remove my shift. I use AI daily for manuals, but a search result does not tell me whether the glue has actually held.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the laminator and peeling a sample from the first bonded sheet of each run. I would use my usual daily AI manual and fault-log tools, checking the results against the approved specification. At the next union shift meeting I would ask whether quicker paperwork changes line targets or paid sample time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our present income. A tidy log is good; a pallet of board that peels apart is not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a failed peel test look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The layers separate cleanly instead of tearing fibres, which tells me the bond is weak. I stop the line and check glue temperature before another pallet is stacked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask the union about sample time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A faster order system sometimes comes with a new pallet target. I want the delegate to get the test interval and staffing in writing at the scheduled meeting.

say: A quicker **paper order** still needs physical peel testing.
The **sample interval** should not vanish under a new target.
think: Current **household wages** and three months saved cover ordinary costs.
Office AI does not yet replace my **laminator shift**.
do: **Keep** tuning glue and peel-testing first bonded sheets.
**Use** existing daily AI manual searches with specification checks.
**Ask** union meeting for written targets and paid sample time.
feel: **Calm** while the physical line and present household pay remain sound.
S0.quote: The bonded board still has to pass a peel test before I release a pallet.
fieldNote: His **senior process skill** covers heat, glue and crew instruction, while a physical peel test remains the release check.
His **daily AI use** is existing manual and log work; the union request concerns actual paid sample time.

steps.text: Keep tuning laminator and peel-testing first bonded sheets
Ask scheduled union shift meeting for written targets and paid test time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can schedule paper rolls before a robot can load them and clear a glue spill. If we get a bond camera, I want a paid guarded trial, actual false-reject results and the proposed shift roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be glad to try it, but the plant might cut a sample-check shift and reduce our ordinary household wage. Three months saved and Marek's counter pay offer a little room, not a permanent replacement. My current AI manual search is not the same as knowing the new camera controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request the proposed roster and a guarded paid camera trial with the process technician. If offered, I would learn the AI bond-alert display by testing good and deliberately under-glued scrap board, comparing the alerts with peel tests. If paid hours actually fall, I would apply to posted safe local packaging-machine or quality jobs only where guaranteed wages after travel and shift times cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about an hours cut, although I want the test. The camera should prove its bond check before it counts as a reason to lose a checker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you make a useful bad sample?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The technician could lower glue feed on scrap board, then reset the approved setting. I would pull the layers apart and compare the camera flag with the fibre tear while guards remain shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a nearby plant advertises a higher rate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check whether the posted base wage after travel still covers costs at its actual hours. An optional bonus cannot be the only reason to leave a paid shift.

say: I would request a **paid guarded camera trial** and real roster.
The **bond alert** must agree with peel tests on scrap board.
think: A lost **sample-check shift** could reduce household income.
Three months **saved** and Marek's pay allow only temporary adjustment.
do: **Request** proposed roster and offered paid guarded bond-camera trial.
**Learn** AI bond alerts only on supervised scrap-board practice.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe local packaging at viable net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible paid-hour loss despite eagerness to test.
S1.quote: The camera should prove its bond check before it counts as a reason to lose a checker.
fieldNote: His **new AI learning** requires active supervised guarded bond-camera practice, beyond established daily manual searches.
A **job move** follows actual hours lost and a real safe local posting with bill-covering net wages.

steps.text: Request proposed roster and offered paid guarded bond-camera trial
Learn AI bond alerts only if supervised guarded scrap practice offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our union branch AGI could plan carton orders in 2028, while capable robots that load paper and run the laminator arrive around 2031. We need paid technical places and a written staffing schedule before that equipment is ordered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 at the physical robot date. I expect much of the roll-handling and sampling work, including my lead shift, to disappear; the few local packaging plants might change as well. Three months saved would run down quickly if I lost my wage, and I have been awake wondering how we would meet housing costs in month four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would put off replacing the dining-room floor and hold that money for bills. I would attend the union's scheduled bargaining meeting to press for funded paid places and retained jobs. I would enrol in a locally accepted packaging-quality certificate only if fees, paid release and supervised guarded laminator lockout practice are funded. After passing and losing shifts, I would apply to posted safe local quality jobs only if guaranteed base pay after travel and hours covers costs; without a course place, I would apply to posted safe packaging-machine jobs on the same terms while keeping paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by a likely major loss of paid work. A technical diploma will not keep the rent paid if no local position is posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a practical quality course teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would measure a weak bond, record the glue setting and isolate the stopped laminator before clearing a jam. A trainer must watch me with the guard closed and lockout checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if written retirement income, Marek's reliable wages and our costs add up after housing, food and health needs. We have not verified that, so I would seek paid jobs.

say: I would separate **2028 planning AGI** from physical laminator robots around 2031.
Our union should secure **paid technical places** before installation.
think: At **63**, lead shifts and hands-on sample work may disappear.
Three months **saved** cannot fund a long search for scarce local posts.
do: **Delay** the dining-room floor and keep cash for bills.
**Attend** union bargaining for funded paid places and retained jobs.
**Enrol** only in accepted guarded packaging training, then apply to posted local jobs at viable net pay.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless housing worries.
S2.quote: A technical diploma will not keep the rent paid if no local position is posted.
fieldNote: His **2031 risk** is robots handling physical rolls and samples after AGI first changes order planning.
The **quality and machine applications** require real safe local postings with base wages after travel and shifts covering costs.
Require **safe posted work** with guaranteed pay after travel and shifts covering bills; qualified inspection or machine fallback.

Apply after cuts to safe posted quality-if-qualified/machine-otherwise jobs only with guaranteed bill-covering after-travel pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI might plan packaging orders in 2031 while capable robots reach the laminator around 2034. Five years gives us time to settle an accepted paid course and look at the actual local job board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 when those robots arrive. Marek and I could choose to stop sooner if written retirement income covers our household costs, but three months saved does not prove that. My technical skill may suit process inspection if a paid vacancy actually exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would add a new amount from full paid months to savings after bills and ask the union at its next meeting to seek paid release for quality places. I would enrol only if a nearby employer accepts the certificate and a funded place includes supervised guarded laminator lockout. After passing and losing hours, I would apply to posted safe local inspection jobs only if guaranteed pay after travel and shifts covers bills; if no course place opens, I would apply to posted safe packaging-machine work on the same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about getting from a class to a real wage. Five years is useful only if the course and job are both there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check acceptance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the credential with current nearby inspection postings and ask each plant about supervised laminator practice. If none accepts it, I would ask for another funded place instead of taking an empty certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you actually stop work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek and I would compare written income with housing, food, transport and likely health costs. If it reliably covers them, I would leave before the robot shift change; otherwise I would keep earning and applying.

say: I would seek a **paid accepted course** before 2034 robots.
Actual **local postings** must establish a paid route after training.
think: At **66**, early retirement depends on written income after costs.
The **technical diploma** helps only if a vacancy pays for the skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI could plan carton orders in 2036, while capable robots reach the physical laminator around 2039. Ten years gives us a chance to see whether a written retirement budget can replace my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 71 when robots arrive, if I am still working. Our current wages and three months saved cover bills today; Marek and I might stop earlier, but only if written income covers housing and health costs. We have not run that arithmetic yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking safe paid laminator shifts and request written retirement-income estimates beside a full cost list this year. If I still need wages, I would enrol in a locally accepted packaging-quality course only when funded fees, paid release and supervised guarded practice are offered. If I remain employed after 2036 and paid hours fall, I would apply only to posted safe nearby packaging or inspection jobs whose guaranteed wages after travel and shift times cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long decision, while current household pay still covers us. I would rather know the budget than guess how long a machine job lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an earlier exit affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek and I would compare written income with rent, food, transport and likely health costs. If the reliable total covers them, I would stop before 2039; if not, I would keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for an online certificate yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would need a funded paid place with a trainer and guarded laminator practice. Without that, I keep the wage and check posted local jobs after any cuts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 AGI and 2031 robot picture worries me most because the laminator shifts could disappear before Marek and I know if stopping work is affordable. An accepted funded practical course, a negotiated staffing timetable and real posted safe local jobs at bill-covering pay after travel would help. I would keep taking paid work until another route exists.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who pulls a weak sheet off the top of a finished stack. A pallet can look straight while its cardboard layers are already separating.

headlineQuote: A pallet can look straight while its cardboard layers are already separating.
portrait: **Emeka**, 58, is a senior corrugated-board laminator lead with a two-year technical diploma and exceptional process skill.
He and his **partner Marek** have grown children, typical lead pay, three months saved and some other packaging plants nearby.
He uses **AI daily** for manuals and logs, checks real peel tests and supports union bargaining for paid practical training.
Expected **2031 physical robots** threaten laminator shifts; an earlier stop requires verified retirement income covering actual costs.
biggestWorry: **2031 laminator robots** could remove his senior paid shift before affordable retirement or a viable local wage is clear.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **accepted funded guarded training**, negotiated staffing dates and posted safe local jobs with adequate net pay.
